paper_title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: GPU kernels are one of the main levers on the efficiency of large language model training and serving (Miao et al., 2025). Attention is the clearest case: each GPU generation has required new implementation to reach the hardwares potential, from FlashAttention on Ampere (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024) to FlashAttention-3 on Hopper (Shah et al., 2024) and FlashAttention-4 on Blackwell (Zadouri et al., 2026), each rewrite reporting 1.52 speedup over its predecessor (Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024), and serving systems ship specialized attention engines of their own (Kwon et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2024). Such kernels are deep targets: their performance hinges on whole-pipeline choreography (warp-specialized producers and consumers, asynchronous tensor-core MMAs, copies ordered by barrier phases, register budgets, persistent schedulers, the host dispatch path) rather than on local edits, their correctness hinges on hardware invariants that documentation states 1Snowflake AI Research 2Carnegie Mellon University. Correspondence to: Gabriele Oliaro <goliaro@cs.cmu.edu>. Preprint. only in passing, and they must win across production feature surface of paged caches, grouped heads, masks, ragged batches, split decode, and low precision rather than on one shape. Domain-specific languages (Tillet et al., 2019; Spector et al., 2025) and template libraries (Thakkar et al., 2023) lower the barrier, but state-of-the-art kernels still take expert teams months per architecture (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), and NVIDIAs own production kernels sit well below the hardwares speed of light on many shapes (Lin et al., 2026). Kernel generation has therefore become an active application of LLM coding agents, with benchmarks (Ouyang et al., 2025; Xing et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Oliaro et al., 2026), models trained with reinforcement learning to emit kernels (Baronio et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), agentic pipelines (Hong et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026a), evolutionary search with an LLM as the mutation operator (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026), and deployments across whole production backends (Liao et al., 2025; Cursor & NVIDIA, 2026). These agents sit at the two ends of structurefreedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix in advance Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization what the model does at each step: generatetestrefine loop with learned policy (Baronio et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), menu of optimizations (Hong et al., 2025), team with fixed roles (Wei et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026a), or harness in which humans gate every promotion (Shui et al., 2026). The script makes them sample-efficient but encodes what to try: Autocomps performance collapses without its optimization menu (Hong et al., 2025), and fixedloop RL that is competitive on single operators fails on fused models (Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Open-ended agents let an LLM mutate population of programs (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2025; Wiedemann et al., 2026), and AVO makes self-directed coding agent the variation operator itself (Chen et al., 2026). The freedom buys results, up to 10.5% over FA4 for AVO (Chen et al., 2026) and 32% speedup of FlashAttention kernel for AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), and is paid for in trials: AVOs agent explored more than 500 directions over seven days to commit 40 versions and needed supervisor to break cycles of failing edits (Chen et al., 2026), about 30% of the lines such agents add are byte-identical to lines they deleted earlier (Pelleriti et al., 2026), and 3055% of LLM-evolved CUDA candidates are incorrect (Guo et al., 2025; Varadharajan et al., 2026). We argue that what both ends lack is direction: hypothesis about where the remaining gap is. script hard-codes direction and cannot supply it where the script is wrong; open-ended search samples for it, and samples poorly, because LLMs are not open-ended optimizers. They search greedily from their priors (Redko et al., 2026), anchor on the solution in the prompt (Jones & Steinhardt, 2022), stop early out of conservatism or after run of failures (Merouani et al., 2025), cycle through near-duplicate variants (Li et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025), and report completion the environment contradicts (Advani, 2026). Information is not what is missing: both ends already hand the agent profilers, documentation, and reference implementations (Chen et al., 2026; MIT HAN Lab, 2026), and such feedback helps only when it supplies the specific thing the model lacks, which profiler and compiler output rarely does (Redko et al., 2026). What moves the same models is hypothesis posed from outside: intrinsic self-correction fails where external feedback succeeds (Huang et al., 2024), humans feedback on models own code raised repair success by 1.57 through structural changes the model did not propose (Olausson et al., 2024), and in the FlashInfer kernel contest, agents given expert directions beat the same agents running alone on every kernel (Shui et al., 2026). Our reading, and our traces, say that question changes the task. Make this faster is open-ended, and the model answers it greedily. Is the baseline winning on kernel cycles or only on wallclock? is bounded, and to answer it the model will tear Figure 1. KERNELSEEK vs. scripted, tool-rich autonomous agent on the same FA3 case-study task: the same evaluator, 26 configurations, H200 node, and week. Lines are the lineages best geomean (solid) and worst configuration (dashed); dots are individual candidates; ticks mark human turns to KERNELSEEK. The equipped agents model was active for the 62 hours shown; the shaded band is period with no KERNELSEEK activity. out and rewrite part of the kernel it would never touch on its own. well-placed question supplies direction without narrowing what the agent may do next, which neither more structure, more freedom, nor more tooling can. This paper presents KERNELSEEK, question-driven agent for optimizing CUDA kernels. KERNELSEEK takes an existing kernel as its seed and makes it faster; it is not tied to an operator, and it does not need faster implementation to imitate. It keeps the freedom of the open-ended agents, general-purpose coding agent with no script and no pre-digested context, and recovers the efficiency of the scripted ones by supplying direction at decision points: when progress stalls, when the agent claims limit or completion, and after suspiciously large wins. Its only purposebuilt component is minimal harness that checks every candidate against the seeds outputs and an fp32 reference, times every scenario against the seed, and states the goal as stop condition that is verified rather than requested. good question contains no answer: it names hypothesis the agent has not considered, and testing it takes measurement the agent can make with ordinary tools. Questions that recur harden into bank the agent applies to itself, and KERNELSEEK composes with evolutionary search by wrapping the same agent in an AVO-style lineage whose directives are questions. We evaluate KERNELSEEK on case study chosen because strong upstream exists to measure against: FA3Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization and FA4-class attention kernels as single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, across the feature surface that vLLM exposes, with the upstream kernels as correctness oracle and yardstick. Against an autonomous agent we built for the same task in the style of AVO and its successors, with an orchestrated loop, predigested profiles, documentation retrieval, and store of learned lessons, KERNELSEEK reached 1.13 FA3 in geometric mean over the same 26 configurations on the same machine in the same week, where the autonomous agent plateaued at 0.50 after 133 model-driven steps (Figure 1). Carried through to full campaigns, KERNELSEEK produced fa3 hopper.cu and fa4 blackwell.cu, correct on all 182 Hopper and all runnable Blackwell scenarios, at 1.16 FA3 and 1.46 FA4 in geomean, including 1.10 FA4 on production shapes from SOL-ExecBench (Lin et al., 2026). Across the 16 sessions that produced them, KERNELSEEK made 11.5K tool calls per 162 human messages: asking did not mean using fewer tools, but using them on the right thing. This paper makes three contributions. We identify the failure modes of autonomous agents on deep kernel targets that neither more structure, more freedom, nor more tooling fixes, and show them co-occurring in tool-rich agent built to the prevailing recipe (3). We present KERNELSEEK, an operator-agnostic questiondriven kernel agent built from minimal harness, verifiable goal, and reusable question bank, and show how it composes with evolutionary search (2). We compare KERNELSEEK with the equipped agent on the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, analyze 162 human messages and 11.5K tool calls to show which questions redirected the agent and why (5), and release fa3 hopper.cu and fa4 blackwell.cu, to our knowledge the fastest open-source FA3and FA4class forward kernels on the scenarios we evaluate, with the harness, question bank, and complete traces of both approaches (4).

sections.title: KERNEL AGENT
sections.content: KERNELSEEK takes working CUDA kernel, set of scenarios, and goal, and returns faster kernel whose outputs match the seed on every scenario. It has three parts: minimal harness that makes the goal verifiable, generalpurpose coding agent with no script around it, and source of questions at the moments the agent is about to go wrong. The questions come from human steerer or, once they recur, from bank the agent applies to itself. Nothing in the method is specific to an operator, and nothing requires faster implementation to exist.

sections.title: 2.1 Ask vs. Equip: A Common Frame
sections.content: Kernel optimization by an agent is search. candidate is kernel source; its fitness is vector of per-scenario speedups over the seed, collapsed to zero if any scenario is incorrect; and the lineage is monotone, as in AVO (Chen et al., 2026). The agent is the variation operator: it proposes the next candidate conditioned on context, and everything designer can do is choice of what enters that context and when. An equipped agent receives the task, tools whose output has been distilled for it (a profiler parser that names the bottleneck, disassembly differ), knowledge retrieved for it (documentation sections, hints mined from reference libraries, store of lessons), the lineage, and feedback on the last candidate; the designer improves it by adding tools and knowledge. Our baseline (3) is serious instance. An asked agent receives the task, the harnesss output, the lineage, and, at decision points, short question. It still has every tool developer machine offers, the compiler, profiler, disassembler, sanitizer, and debugger, but nothing is predigested, and direction arrives as question rather than menu. The designer improves it by asking better questions.

sections.title: 2.2 A Minimal Harness and a Verifiable Goal
sections.content: The only component we build is the evaluator. One command builds candidate, checks its outputs against the seeds and an fp32 reference on every scenario, and times it against the seed back to back on the same GPU, reporting per-scenario ratios and their geometric mean. Other kernels the user cares about can be added as measured comparison columns, but none is required. Constraints are stated once and enforced mechanically: in the case study, the ban on CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, and cuDNN is checked by inspecting the built binarys symbols. The goal is predicate over the evaluators output, enforced rather than requested. We install it as Stop hook in the coding agent: whenever the agent attempts to end its turn, the hook evaluates the predicate and, if any clause is unmet, returns the agent to work with the unmet clauses in hand. predicate such as at least parity with the seed on every scenario removes the most common failure of autonomous agents, declaring completion early. Two lessons shaped how we write predicates. They must quantify over every scenario rather than an aggregate, because an agent will otherwise satisfy the aggregate on the shapes it is good at. And they must not be judged by model where they can be computed: the one time our hook delegated the verdict to model judge, it accepted premature claim that human then overturned (5.4). Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization

sections.title: 2.3 Questions: What They Are and When to Ask
sections.content: Across the traces, the questions that preceded the largest gains share six properties. They carry no answer: they name class of hypothesis and leave the derivation to the agent. They demand measurement the agent can make with the tools it has, so the answer is number rather than an opinion. They move across layers of the system, from the kernel to the host launch path to the routing logic to the benchmark itself, where an agent left alone stays at the layer it started at. They refuse premature closure by asking whether claimed limit is property of the hardware or of the agents own design. They are cheap, tens of tokens against the tens of thousands that retrieved documentation costs (Liu et al., 2024; LangChain, 2025). And they counteract deference: an agent tends to keep the structure it started from and accept the framing it is given (Sharma et al., 2024), and question asks it to justify that choice with evidence. Eight categories cover the questions human asked during the case study (Table 4 in Appendix A): measurement check (13 messages), bound differencing (10), benchmark validity (7), gap triage (7), agent process (6), challenge limit (5), strategy options (5), and hypothesis check (3). The largest checks measurement: whether win is noise, whether comparison is fair, whether the agent is timing what it thinks it is timing. The second pits the agents claimed ceiling against an independent estimate of what is achievable. In the case study that estimate was often the upstream kernel, but the pattern does not depend on one existing: roofline, speed-of-light figure (Lin et al., 2026), or an A/B that swaps only the launcher around an identical binary serves the same role. Questions are asked at decision points, not continuously; the traces show five: at the start of campaign, to fix the scope; at plateau; when the agent claims limit or completion; after suspiciously large win; and when correctness breaks in way the agent explains away. Between these points the agent works alone, about 71 tool calls per human message, where the median message is sentence or two. The steerer contributes no code and no CUDA knowledge the agent lacks; it contributes doubt, at the right moment, about the right thing.

sections.title: 2.4 The Question Bank
sections.content: After the campaigns we distilled the recurring questions into bank. Its first version, taken from the traces alone, had 48 entries, and reading it back showed the hazard of distilling from one case study: 21 named the upstream kernel as the comparison and 13 named attention structure. The released bank removes both. question is admitted only if it carries no answer, is answerable by measurement with stock tools, is phrased against bound (a roofline or per-tile cycle budget) rather than reference, names an architecture only as parameter, and names no operator. To cover the aspects single attention campaign never exercised, we also mined three public GEMM worklogs on Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell (Boehm, 2022; Shankhdhar, 2024; Modular Inc., 2025) and the FlashAttention-3 and -4 papers (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026) for the diagnostic that preceded each of their optimizations, and phrased it as question. The result has 101 core entries in ten groups ordered by where the gap might be (scope and triage; the bound and the regime; harness and measurement; host, launch, and routing; memory hierarchy; compute issue; occupancy and registers; asynchrony and pipelining; scheduling; low-precision numerics), five that apply only when another implementation is available to measure, and eighteen per-architecture checklist entries that bind the generic mechanisms to Ampere, Hopper, or Blackwell instructions. Operator structure enters through plug-in with five slots (regimes, irregular work, non-MMA units, reduction splits, indirect loads); the attention plug-in fills them with prefill and decode, causal masks, softmax, split-KV, and paged gathers. Appendix lists the bank with provenance tags: 29 entries carry trace tag, and the 72 from public sources alone are untested.

sections.title: 2.5 From Asking the Agent to the Agent Asking Itself
sections.content: Because the questions recur, they can be handed to the agent as part of its instructions. We codify them as skill with five parts: the goal, the hard rules the harness enforces, loop, list of questions to ask itself, and the commands that run the evaluator and profiler. The loop is the bank in procedural form: fix the scope; measure the seed; classify each gap as host, routing, or kernel before touching code; bound it; form hypothesis; rewrite; gate. At each step the agent fans out subagents, one per hypothesis, each returning hypothesis and the measurement that tests it rather than patch. The skill is parameterized by the seed, the scenario set, and the goal; its questions were reused across the Hopper and Blackwell campaigns nearly verbatim.

sections.title: 2.6 Composing with Evolutionary Search
sections.content: KERNELSEEK is compatible with the evolutionary loops of the open-ended agents, because it changes the variation operators direction rather than the loop around it. We wrap the same agent in an AVO-style search (Chen et al., 2026): monotone lineage, several diverse mutations per generation applied to isolated copies and scored by the evaluator, and strategist that reviews the trajectory and writes the next generations directives. The one change is that the directives are questions, hypotheses to test rather than edits to make. As 5.5 shows, evolution amplifies direction; it does not supply it. Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization

sections.title: 2.7 Hypotheses
sections.content: The evaluation tests five claims. H1 (quality): on the same task, evaluator, and hardware, the asked agent reaches higher performance at full correctness than the equipped one. H2 (efficiency): with fewer model-driven steps and GPU-hours, counting human time. H3 (mechanism): the largest gains follow questions that change the layer under consideration or reject claimed limit, not questions that supply information. H4 (complementarity): evolutionary search amplifies the effect of questions and does not substitute for them. H5 (generality): the questions that moved the case study contain nothing specific to the operator or to reference once the reference is replaced by bound.

sections.title: AUTONOMOUS EVOLUTIONARY AGENT
sections.content: Before KERNELSEEK, we built the agent the prevailing recipe prescribes. ARSENAL is an autonomous evolutionary agent for the Hopper half of the case study (4), in the lineage of AVO, KDA, and CUCo (Chen et al., 2026; MIT HAN Lab, 2026; Varadharajan et al., 2026): an orchestrated loop, profiler whose output is distilled for the model, retrieval over documentation and reference libraries, typed knowledge store, and no human in the loop by design. Its failure is the papers motivation, and its evaluator, unchanged, scored the first KERNELSEEK session in the head-to-head of 5.3. Design. The task was single dependency-free CUDA file implementing vLLMs FA3 operator for H200, with success defined as at least parity with FA3 on 26 configurations and token-for-token equality with FA3 on greedy decode in vLLM. deterministic Python orchestrator owns the loop. Each step generates one candidate, builds it, checks for forbidden dependencies by inspecting the binarys symbols, analyzes the SASS instruction mix, verifies correctness on all 26 configurations, times it against FA3 interleaved across four GPUs, profiles the worst configuration with NCU, and, on promotion, A/B-tests it inside live vLLM instance. It then writes lesson to memory file, note to the knowledge store, and an entry to lever ledger, checks for plateau, and checkpoints. Claude Opus model (claude-opus-4-8) running headless in Claude Code is the brain, invoked in fresh session at every step. The orchestrator decides what to try and the brain decides how: sixteen hand-written levers, from tensor-core MMAs and TMA loads to warp specialization and persistent scheduling, are keyed to the bottleneck label the NCU parser assigns, and the chosen lever is placed in the prompt with the instruction to write the improved candidate. Everything else the brain sees is distilled by component (Appendix E): bottleneck diagnosis, retrieved documentation, hints extracted from DeepGEMM, ThunderKittens, and CUTLASS, and typed knowledge-store notes. The median step prompt was 22.6K characters, 37% of it pre-fetched reference material, plus the current best kernel re-read each step. Promotion is greedy on the worst-case configuration ratio with 3% noise band, and plateau detector opens rewrite branches. No human-authored text ever entered step prompt. Outcome. The run kept 313 steps over 4.2 days, with further 117 discarded by three human rollbacks. The model was active for steps 0 to 132, about 62 hours and $660 of API usage over 253 sessions; from step 133 the brains credentials had expired and the loop re-scored old kernels until stopped, so we report 133 model-driven steps as the budget. The best candidate reached 0.50 FA3 in geometric mean with worst case of 0.24; no configuration reached parity. All progress happened by step 35, in about 45 hours. The remaining 98 model-driven steps produced nothing beyond noise: the final champion, from step 112, is byte-identical to the candidate of step 104 and was promoted because one of 54 re-measurements of the same source landed above the noise band. Correctness was not the problem: 312 of 313 candidates were correct. Why it stalled. The traces show the failure modes of 1, each with number attached. Information was not the constraint: with more than third of every prompt devoted to reference material and 1.6 GB of reference code on disk, 82% of the characters the brain read through its own tool calls were its own kernel, and its 92 documentation lookups over 246 sessions mostly justified not making change. The menu bounded the search: 36 of the 37 rewrite branches the plateau detector opened were seeded from the same step, and every candidate after step 35 was local edit of the same design. Memory hardened conclusions, not evidence: the memory file recorded one configuration as DEFINITIVE[ly] . . . walled by [the] 65536-reg file, wall FA3 does not hit, and the brains summary at step 112 was that the only remaining escape is clean-sheet 1-blk/SM warpspec persistent seed, which is outside this branchs mandate and measured to lose; each fresh session inherited earlier verdicts without the reasoning behind them, and nothing in the loop was positioned to doubt them. Every diagnostic lived at one layer: NCU, the SASS analyzer, and the sanitizer all examine the kernel, while the gap KERNELSEEK later closed on this evaluator was in the host launch path (5.4). The objective rewarded caution: promoting on the worst configuration inside noise band accepted noise as progress and could not fund restructuring that regresses before it pays off; 312 correct candidates out of 313 is the signature of search that never took risk. Three lessons carried into KERNELSEEK: the mechanical parts of the harness were worth keeping, and KERAsk, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization NELSEEKs harness is this evaluator with the orchestration removed; everything built to inform the brain could go, and the knowledge store was actively harmful; and the loop lacked one input, reason to doubt conclusion and hypothesis about where else to look.

FLASHATTENTION FOR HOPPER AND
BLACKWELL
sections.content: Task. We asked KERNELSEEK to produce FlashAttention forward kernel for Hopper and one for Blackwell, each single CUDA file with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, exposing the operator schema vLLM uses for FlashAttention-3 so that the result drops in for the upstream kernel and is timed against it from identical inputs. The scenario suites mirror the upstream kernels own test grids and add production shapes from SOL-ExecBench (Lin et al., 2026): 182 scenarios per architecture spanning bf16, fp16, and fp8; paged and contiguous KV caches; MHA, GQA, and MQA; causal, sliding-window, softcapped, and attentionsink masking; ragged batches; prefill, chunked prefill, and split-KV decode; and unequal query and value head dimensions. The breadth is deliberate, since kernels scored on few shapes report speedups that shrink on the production path (Oliaro et al., 2026). The goal was correctness on every scenario and at least parity with upstream in geometric mean. The seed in both cases was slow but general kernel (a scalar one-warp-per-query kernel on Hopper, onewarpgroup dense-only skeleton on Blackwell), and anything the fast paths did not yet cover fell back to it, so correctness held throughout. The upstream kernels, FA3 as shipped in vLLM and the CuteDSL FA4 (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), were the correctness oracle and the yardstick the goal was stated against. The dependency-free constraint means the layouts, descriptors, pipelines, and register allocation that CUTLASS and CuteDSL derive for the upstream kernels had to be written by hand (Thakkar et al., 2023). Both kernels are correct on every scenario they run, and both beat upstream in geometric mean. fa3 hopper.cu runs at 1.16 FA3 with 135 of 182 scenarios at or above parity; the wins are concentrated in ragged prefill, paged and speculative decode, and the masking grid, while the paper-style sweeps of the claim set are at parity and dense fp8 prefill is the one clear hole at 0.67. fa4 blackwell.cu runs at 1.46 FA4 across the 124 scenarios FA4 also runs, with 98 at or above parity and worst case of 0.78. The headline shrinks as the baseline strengthens: cuDNN is the fastest baseline on 54 of 182 Hopper scenarios and on 92 of 124 Blackwell ones, where it wins dense prefill and batched decode outright, so the kernels are 1.10 and 1.07 the fastest available Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization implementation, and at or above it on production shapes. Three caveats are documented in Appendix B: the edge sets consist of short kernels, so part of their 1.52 is upstream dispatch overhead; the largest claim wins are fp8-KV decode shapes on which FA4 is slow, and excluding them moves the Blackwell all-set geomeans to 1.37, 1.32, and 1.08; and one paged-KV fast path depends on physically consecutive pages. Every Blackwell scenario below parity has measured cause: dense long context spends identical tensor work over third more cycles because of twice as many barrier waits per block, batched decode pays cold start per CTA, and head dimension 96 runs on padded 128-wide path. On Hopper the losses are fp8 dense prefill, softcapped prefill, head dimension 96, and long sliding windows (0.340.79); these have not been profiled to the same depth. Release. We release both kernels under Apache 2.0 with the evaluator, the PTX probes used to validate each Blackwell primitive in isolation, the search scripts (2.6), the question bank and skill, and the complete agent traces of both approaches. The kernels are meant as seeds, with their residual gaps measured, so that the next agent starts from known frontier.

sections.title: 5.2 RQ1: Kernel Performance
sections.content: The kernels are reported in 4. In brief: fa3 hopper.cu is correct on all 182 Hopper scenarios at 1.16 FA3 and 1.10 the fastest available implementation including cuDNN; fa4 blackwell.cu is correct on all 154 runnable Blackwell scenarios at 1.46 FA4 and 1.07 the fastest available. Per-scenario Hopper ratios vary by 1% at the median and 6% at most across repeats. Every Blackwell scenario below parity has measured root cause (Appendix B). This is H1s quality half, and the result the rest of the section explains. Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization

sections.title: 5.3 RQ2: Head-to-Head on the Same Task
sections.content: The comparison is controlled in the ways that matter. During its first Hopper session, KERNELSEEK adopted the equipped agents own evaluator, the same 26 configurations, FA3 baseline, and correctness gate, on the same machine, in overlapping days. Table 2 and Figure 1 give the outcome. The equipped agents lineage champion reached 0.48 FA3 at step 35, after 44.7 hours, and did not improve in the remaining 98 model-driven steps (3). Its worst configuration stayed at 0.24 and none reached parity. KERNELSEEK started from 0.009, because its kernel of the time routed the evaluators paged and grouped-query configurations to the scalar fallback, and reached 0.96 after 21 hours, 1.02 after 66, and 1.13 after 68, of which 26.7 were an idle gap. At the end, 22 of 26 configurations were at or above parity and the worst was 0.87. This supports H1 and, counting the 40 human turns against 133 steps and 62 model-hours, H2. Three caveats qualify the comparison: KERNELSEEK had built kernel for FA3s 40-scenario test grid in the two preceding days, so the 0.009 start understates its head start; the front-ends differ, and token usage is not recoverable for the Cursor sessions; and each arm is single run. The fair reading is that in one calendar week steered agent crossed parity on an evaluator on which an unsteered one, given more compute, did not reach half of it. We treat Table 2 as showing that the gap exists and is large, and RQ3 as the evidence for why. Where the effort went. The lower block of Table 2 contrasts tool use. The equipped agent received third of its context as pre-fetched reference material, yet spent 82% of what it read on its own kernel. KERNELSEEK, with nothing pushed to it, spent 26% on its own kernels and ran the profiler 429 times on raw output. The questions did not reduce tool use; they aimed it. Which questions mattered. Table 3 walks through six turning points we can verify in the archived traces. Two patterns stand out. First, every large jump followed question that either moved the agent to different layer (from kernel tuning to the per-configuration table, to the host launch path, to the benchmark itself) or rejected claimed limit; none followed message that supplied information the agent lacked, which supports H3. Second, the measurement the question triggered was always one the agent could already make: the per-configuration table, the host-side profile, the sanitizer, and the debugger were available at every earlier step. What the agent lacked was reason to look. Four further episodes, among them the 38 µs host copy and routing sweep that moved the Blackwell geomean from 0.88 to 1.15 without changing kernel body, are documented in the repositorys history but not in archived sessions, and we cite them as outcomes only.

sections.title: 5.5 RQ4: Questions and Evolutionary Search
sections.content: We wrapped the same agent in the loop of 2.6 and ran it on the Blackwell dense-prefill kernel from correct but slow port (Figure 3, Appendix D). The first generation, whose directive asked whether persistent schedule with longestfirst ordering and cross-tile overlap would recover the lost overlap, took the kernel from 0.29 to 0.68. Three more generations added 0.10 between them through folded softmax scale, split K/V barrier, and depth-two softmax correction handshake, while directives on register rebalancing and address hoisting measured neutral or negative. The search stalled at 0.78 with the kernels own cycle count already below upstreams. The last 22 points came from question, not generation: asked where the time was going, the agent profiled the whole call rather than the kernel and found that synchronous host copies accounted for the gap. Evolution amplified the direction the directives carried and searched efficiently within the layer it was pointed at; it could not move to layer it was not pointed at. This is H4.

sections.title: 5.6 RQ5: Reuse
sections.content: What the human said. Of the 162 human messages, directives are the largest class (58, 36%), followed by questions (44, 27%), approvals (30, 19%), corrections (19, 12%), and goals (11, 7%); 63 messages (39%) are interrogative in phrasing, and 12 of the 19 corrections are phrased as questions (Appendix D). The steering was interrogative, not mostly questions: directives and approvals keep the agent moving, and the questions are where its course changed. The agent also asked. Across the Claude Code sessions it posed 35 structured questions to the human, 24 of which offered an option to accept the current state or stop, and its messages assert limit or an impossibility 126 times. The Stop hook returned it to work 59 times. Autonomous agents seek closure; the harness and the human refused it. The question categories were populated mostly during the Hopper campaign, which came first. Five of the eight recur in the Blackwell campaign, and the Blackwell skills selfquestions restate Hopper questions nearly verbatim. Of the 63 interrogative messages, 17 mention concept specific to attention and 32 mention the upstream kernel; the rest name only measurements, layers, and process, and where question names the upstream it uses it as bound, role roofline fills when no upstream exists. This is the evidence for H5 that we have: necessary, since bank that did not transfer across two architectures would not transfer further, but not sufficient, since both campaigns were attention and the 72 bank entries mined from public sources (2.4) have not yet steered an agent. sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Did human expert do the work? The human wrote no kernel code, and the messages name measurements, layers, and process rather than mechanisms: of the 63 interrogative ones, 17 mention an attention concept and none prescribes CUDA construct (5.6). The human did have systems expertise and used it to decide which measurement to demand and when; we claim only that the questions, once asked, are short, generic, and now written down. The agent wrote all 13.8K lines of the two kernels. Whether the bank can replace the human is the experiment this paper does not contain. Its design is fixed: start from the released Blackwell kernel on one of its remaining gaps (dense long context or head dimension 96), hold the model and budget constant, and compare four arms: the equipped loop, the bare agent with the harness alone, the bare agent with questioner that draws from the bank at plateaus and claimed limits, and human questioner. Does KERNELSEEK need reference implementation? The method does not: the harness checks correctness against the seed and an fp32 reference, the goal is predicate over the seed, and the bank phrases every bound as roofline or cycle budget. The case study had one, and used it in two roles. As yardstick it set the goal and scored the result. As bound it let question overturn claimed ceiling, and this role is the one that mattered; it is filled without reference by roofline, speed-of-light estimate (Lin et al., 2026), launcher-only A/B, or kernel for neighboring shape, each of which the bank asks for by name. reference buys cheaper and sharper bound, and no more: the equipped agent had far more of it in its prompt and gained nothing. The no-reference campaign, where the seed is the fastest kernel known, is the setting the released agent targets and the one we have not yet run. Threats to validity. The head-to-head is single run per arm, with different front-ends and steered arm against an unsteered one; we control the task, evaluator, hardware, baseline, and correctness gate, and count the human turns in the steered arms budget. The case study is one operator family where strong upstream existed. Wall-clock speedups include dispatch overhead, which inflates the edge sets (Appendix B). The kernels were built before the traces were analyzed, and one author labeled the messages, so the taxonomy may fit the sessions we had; every trace is released so the labeling can be checked. Limitations and future work. The Hopper kernel loses on fp8 dense prefill and softcapped prefill, and the Blackwell kernel does not yet build fp8 inputs or dense head dimensions of 192 and above; neither covers the backward pass. Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization The next targets are other deep kernels (latent-attention decode, grouped GEMMs for mixture-of-experts layers, fused collectives, persistent megakernels (Jin et al., 2026)) and end-to-end evaluation on the production path (Oliaro et al., 2026).

sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: LLM agents for GPU kernels. Benchmarks score single operators (Ouyang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), serving kernels on Blackwell (Xing et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026), production shapes against speed-of-light bound (Lin et al., 2026), and, in FastKernels (Oliaro et al., 2026), agent-written kernels inside the production modules they replace, where kernel-level speedups of several times shrink to at most 1.25 end to end. The systems divide along the structurefreedom axis of 1. Scripted agents train policy inside fixed loop (Baronio et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026), search over menu of optimizations (Hong et al., 2025; Gai et al., 2026), or assign fixed roles to several agents (Wei et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026a; MIT HAN Lab, 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026b). Open-ended agents make an LLM the mutation operator of an evolutionary search (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2025; Wiedemann et al., 2026; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Lange et al., 2025b; Varadharajan et al., 2026) or, in AVO (Chen et al., 2026), self-directed coding agent; Meta (Liao et al., 2025) and Cursor with NVIDIA (Cursor & NVIDIA, 2026) run such loops across whole kernel libraries. AVO is the closest work in target. The closest in spirit is the harness-engineering report of Shui et al. (Shui et al., 2026), which finds that agent-assisted optimization beats fully autonomous agents on every FlashInfer contest kernel but does not isolate what the human contributes. No prior work compares two steering strategies on the same target, evaluator, and hardware. LLMs as optimizers. The failure modes we attribute to autonomous agents are each documented in isolation: greedy, prior-driven search (Redko et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), anchoring on the solution in the prompt (Jones & Steinhardt, 2022), failure to explore without intervention (Krishnamurthy et al., 2024), conservatism and premature stopping (Merouani et al., 2025), early lockin under iterative refinement (Javaji et al., 2025), and false completion claims (Advani, 2026). We show them cooccurring in one well-equipped agent. Questions and self-correction. Self-Ask (Press et al., 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) have the model question itself, but intrinsic self-correction is limited (Huang et al., 2024) and models defer to the framing they are given (Sharma et al., 2024). External feedback works where self-feedback does not: human feedback on models own code raises repair success by more than half, partly because humans propose the structural changes the model does not (Olausson et al., 2024), and stating hypotheses before writing programs improves program synthesis (Wang et al., 2024). These works use questions to improve one answer; we use them to decide what to measure next in long-horizon search, in the tradition of Polyas heuristics (Polya, 1945). Scaffolding, compilers, and kernels. An agents interface moves its performance (Yang et al., 2024), simpler pipelines often win (Xia et al., 2024; Schluntz & Zhang, 2024), and more tools and context have costs (LangChain, 2025; Liu et al., 2024); KERNELSEEK is data point for the second camp with twist, since it used more tools than the equipped agent, but on demand. Korch (Hu et al., 2024) and Event Tensor (Jin et al., 2026) automate different layer, how kernels are grouped and scheduled into persistent megakernels, and are complementary targets for an agent that writes kernel bodies. The kernels we compare against are FlashAttention and its successors (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024; Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), codesigned with CUTLASS (Thakkar et al., 2023); FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025); cuDNN (NVIDIA, 2025); and ThunderKittens (Spector et al., 2025), on the operator surface vLLM defines (Kwon et al., 2023). To our knowledge ours are the first dependency-free FA3and FA4-class kernels to match or exceed upstream across that surface.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: For deep kernel optimization the scarce resource is not information but direction. An autonomous agent equipped with parsed profiler, retrieval, reference material, and knowledge store plateaued at half the speed of FlashAttention-3 after 133 steps on 26-configuration task; the same class of model, given minimal harness and forty messages of which seventeen were questions, passed it in the same week on the same machine. The questions that mattered contained no answers: they moved the agent to layer it had not examined or made it defend limit it had declared. KERNELSEEK packages this: an operator-agnostic agent that makes CUDA seed faster with no faster implementation to imitate, verifiable goal enforced by the harness, question bank the agent applies to itself, and an evolutionary wrapper whose directives are questions. Its case-study output, dependency-free FlashAttention kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, correct on every scenario and faster than upstream, is released with the harness, the bank, and every trace. Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization

sections.title: AI USAGE DISCLOSURE
sections.content: AI coding agents are the subject of this paper, and they produced most of its artifacts. The two kernels, fa3 hopper.cu and fa4 blackwell.cu, were written entirely by the agents described in 2 (Claude Opus models, claude-opus-4-8 and claude-opus-5, run through Claude Code and Cursor) under human steering; no author wrote or edited kernel code. The baseline agent of 3 was itself built by Claude Code from written specification, and its runs used claude-opus-4-8. The evaluator, the search scripts, and the PTX probes were written by the same agents under the same steering. The complete traces of every session are released. The trace analysis of 5 used AI assistance to parse the session logs, classify tool calls by target, and aggregate counts; the human-message labels were assigned by an author. The figures were produced by scripts written with AI assistance from the released data. All reported numbers were re-derived by the authors from the released artifacts. The question bank of Appendix was drafted with AI assistance from the traces and from the public sources it cites, and edited by the authors. The manuscript was drafted and revised with AI writing assistance under the authors direction; the authors specified the argument, structure, and claims, reviewed and rewrote the text, verified every number against the artifacts, and take responsibility for all content. Ask, Dont Equip: Question-Driven Agents for Kernel Optimization

sections.title: A THE FULL QUESTION BANK
sections.content: The bank has three layers. The first is the released bank of 101 core questions plus an operator plug-in (2.3), organized by where performance gap might be and meant to be worked through in order, so that the scope, the bound, the harness, the host, and the routing are settled before the kernel body is touched. The second is the list of questions the skill asks the agent to put to itself at every iteration. The third is the set of question categories observed in the human messages of the case study, with verbatim examples. Every core entry satisfies five admission rules. It carries no answer: it names class of hypothesis or quantity to measure, never technique to apply. It is answerable by measurement with stock tools (the profiler, the disassembler, the assemblers resource report, clock counters, the harness). It is phrased against bound, roofline or per-tile cycle budget, never against reference implementation; the five questions that only make sense when another implementation is available to measure form their own conditional group. It names an architecture only as parameter, and must make sense on Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell alike. And it names no operator: the attention structure the case study needed (paging, softmax, split-KV, grouped heads) lives in plug-in that the template at the end of this section describes. Tags: [G] generic; [A], [H], [B] Ampere-, Hopper-, or Blackwell-specific checklist. Provenance tags give where each question came from: TR, the human messages and skill of our traces; SB, PS, and MO, three public GEMM optimization worklogs on Ampere (Boehm, 2022), Hopper (Shankhdhar, 2024), and Blackwell (Modular Inc., 2025); FA3 and FA4, the FlashAttention-3 and -4 papers (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026). The first bank, distilled from the traces alone after the campaigns, had 48 entries of which 21 named the upstream kernel as the comparison and 13 named attention structure; the released bank is the result of removing both, which moved 11 entries into the plug-in, rewrote 27, kept 10, and added the rest from the public sources. Which bound binds on this scenario (bandwidth, MMA, special-function unit, shared-memory bandwidth, issue slots, launch), and what fraction of it do we reach? 2. Is the gap in kernel cycles, or outside the kernel (host, launch, routing, harness)? 3. Which single unit or stage has the largest excess over its cycle budget, and what is my hypothesis for why? 4. Do the losing scenarios share one cause, and have grouped them before fixing any? 5. Should the losing regime have its own kernel instead of flag in shared one? 6. Is every asynchronous mechanism this architecture offers actually asynchronous in my SASS, or are waits placed where they serialize? 7. Is the win just measured larger than the noise of this GPU at this moment, and does it hold on the other regimes? 8. If another implementation of this operator can be measured on this machine, how do its profile and launch path differ from mine, and which difference explains my gap? A.3 Categories Observed in the Human Messages Table 4 lists the eight categories of 2.3 with verbatim examples from the traces and the outcome they led to where one is documented (5.4). Counts are over the 162 human messages; message is counted in category when its primary act was question or question-shaped correction of that kind. Eight further questions concerned repository housekeeping and are omitted. The fast paths are warpspecialized: one producer warpgroup issues TMA bulktensor loads of and into three-stage shared-memory ring ordered by mbarrier phases, while two consumer warpgroups run asynchronous wgmma MMAs on 128 128 CTA tile, with setmaxnreg moving registers from the producer (40 per thread) to the consumers (up to 168). Prefill is persistent: tiles arrive by TMA, dynamic scheduler hands out tiles, and the two consumer warpgroups ping-pong so that one warpgroups softmax overlaps the others MMAs. Masking is resolved per tile into [lo, hi) key range so that fully visible tiles skip the mask and fully masked tiles exit before the main loop. sections.title: METHODOLOGY
sections.content: Sources. Sixteen KERNELSEEK sessions are archived: nine Claude Code sessions as JSONL transcripts with their subagent transcripts, and seven Cursor sessions as exported JSONL. Claude Code transcripts record the model per assistant message (claude-opus-4-8 in seven sessions, claude-opus-5 in two); Cursor exports do not. The equipped agents run is checkpoint directory with one record per candidate (source, build, correctness, timing, promotion decision, timestamp) and the orchestrators log, memory file, and knowledge store. Parsing. tool call is an assistant content block of type tool use, de-duplicated by its identifier across the parent transcript and any compaction summaries; subagents calls are counted separately and attributed to the parent session. Human turns are user messages that are not tool results, Stop-hook injections, or system reminders; in Cursor exports they are identified by the user records timestamp tag. Tool calls are classified by regular expressions over the tool name and arguments into: profiler runs, SASS or PTX inspections, builds, benchmark or evaluator runs, documentation reads, sanitizer runs, and reads of the agents own kernel files; the categories overlap where shell command does two things. The tool-result text re-reading own kernel figure of Table 2 is the share of tool-result characters returned by file reads whose path is one of the kernel sources, over all tool-result characters in the Claude Code parent transcripts (26%; for the equipped agent, the same quantity over its per-step tool logs, 82%). Figure 4. The 162 human messages across the 16 KERNELSEEK sessions. (a) Primary act. (b) Categories of the 56 messages whose primary act was question, excluding 8 housekeeping questions about the repository. Labeling. One author labeled each of the 162 human messages by its primary act (goal, directive, question, approval, correction), flagged whether it was phrased as question, and assigned the 44 question-act messages and the 12 question-shaped corrections to the categories of 2.3; eight further questions concerned repository housekeeping and are excluded from Figure 4(b). The agent-side counts (35 structured questions to the human, 24 offering to accept or stop, 126 limit assertions, 59 Stop-hook returns) are from the Claude Code sessions only, where these events are structured; the Cursor exports do not separate them. Figure 4 shows the resulting distribution. The labels, the parsing scripts, and the per-session inventory are released with the traces.

The per-step prompt assembled, in order: the task statement and hard rules; the chosen lever with its rationale; the NCU diagnosis for the worst configuration; the SASS instruction-mix deltas against the champion; the retrieved documentation sections; the reference-library hints; the knowledge-store notes matching the lever; the memory files recent lessons; the current champion source; and the instruction to write one improved candidate to fixed path and stop. The median prompt was 22.6K characters excluding the champion source, 37% of it retrieved or pre-fetched material. Promotion required correct candidate whose worst-configuration ratio exceeded the champions by more than 3% noise band. Per-scenario medians over the three repeats are the reported numbers; the four batches agree to within 0.3% on every aggregate, and per-scenario ratios vary by 1% at the median and 6% at most. The Blackwell suite was run once on the 8B200 node with the same protocol. sections.title: F BENCHMARK METHODOLOGY
sections.content: Timing. Each scenario is timed on one GPU with every implementation run back to back from byte-identical inputs. After 20 warm-up calls, the harness takes three trials of 40 CUDA-event samples each, flushing 32 MB buffer through L2 and synchronizing before every sample, and reports the median of the 120 samples; the per-scenario speedup is the upstream median over the implementations median. Clocks are not locked, which is why only ratios are reported. cuDNN and FlashInfer are given the same packed and paged buffers as our kernel and the upstream, and scenario is marked unsupported for an implementation when it rejects the configuration or fails correctness.
